title: Teaching Expertise: Why Great Teachers Think Fast, Slow, and Differently
author: Dr Haili Hughes
summary: Hughes applies Kahneman's 'thinking fast and slow' framework to teacher decision-making, arguing that expert teaching depends on orchestrating both automatic, routine-based judgement (System 1) and deliberate, reflective analysis (System 2). She explains that fast thinking allows teachers to sense confusion or adjust tone almost instinctively, but warns it can also be biased or overconfident, while slow thinking - pausing to ask 'what assumption am I making here?' - drives professional growth but cannot be sustained constantly. Central to her argument is the idea that routine expertise (efficient, familiar moves) and adaptive expertise (flexible responses to the unfamiliar) are mutually reinforcing rather than opposed, developed through reflection-in-action and 'progressive problem-solving' where good teachers keep asking how something that already works could work even better. She closes by arguing CPD must build both technique and the judgement about when, why and how to use it.
points: Hughes's central metaphor - teachers as both 'System 1' and 'System 2' thinkers - reframes classroom decision-making as an orchestration of fast instinct and slow, deliberate analysis rather than a choice between them.
She warns that fast thinking, while necessary for classroom pace, can also produce biased judgements, such as mistaking a student's anxiety or confusion for laziness.

Her concept of 'progressive problem-solving' - expert teachers who 'problematise the unproblematic' by asking how a working strategy could work better - reframes expertise as continuous refinement rather than a fixed endpoint.
She argues CPD implications follow directly: techniques alone are insufficient: teachers need mentoring, coaching and structured reflection to examine when, why and how to use them.
quotes: Some teachers have twenty years of experience, while others have one year of experience repeated twenty times. The difference lies not simply in time served, but in how teachers learn from the complex, unpredictable and deeply human work of teaching.

A teacher may sense that a class is confused before anyone says so. This kind of rapid judgement is not necessarily careless. When developed through rich experience and feedback, it can be a sign of professional competence.
A teacher may assume a student is being lazy when they are actually anxious, confused or overwhelmed. Fast thinking helps teachers survive the pace of the classroom, but it cannot be the whole story.

Expert teachers do not only solve obvious problems; they often problematise the unproblematic. In other words, once something is working, they still ask how it might work better, for more learners, in more meaningful ways.

Great teachers think fast because they have built strong professional routines. They think slow because they know routines are never enough. Most importantly, they keep learning from the space between the two.
